doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Taking on Jane Monheit as a last-stop producer
summary: Dorn tells how Jane Monheit, turned down by everyone, ended up with him and recorded her first album with veteran players.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: You must have a certain reputation in the business.
Is this the trick question I’ve been fearing?
No. I don’t think so. But I’m curious as to how a record label might —
Okay. So that they go for your luck, but how would you get hooked up with like say Jane Monheit for instance? You didn’t like find her, right?

I’ll tell you. See like one thing, I’m 64. I’m not running for class president, I don’t care what anybody thinks basically, so if you ask me a question I’ll tell you the truth. Jane Monheit had been turned down by every major adult producer and record company that exists. By the time they called me, they sent me a demo tape, I turned her down too, the demo tape was terrible. But her manager, Maryann Topra said, “please come hear her in person.” Because I’m telling you, if I would have turned her down, the next person they would have called would have been Stalin, you know? There was nobody left. I really was the last stop on that train you know? And so I went to see her at a club and I saw her live ten seconds and I said naa, she can do it. So we went with it, but it was for like a tiny company, N–coded or something, which was the tattered shards of N2K which was what they did with the money from the sale of GRP to start this new Internet, but whatever it was. So it was a little tiny label, you know, nobody wanted her, and then I threw her in with like real guys: Kenny Barron, Ron Carter, Lewis Nash, Fathead, Hank Crawford. I said look, if I’m going to make a record with her I want to make it with my guys, you know. These are the people I want. Because she’s a retro artist in that she deals with, you know the Classic American Songbook a la the jazz singers of the forties, fifties and sixties, you know. That first record I love. Because she had just turned 22, she was in there with people whose records she had in her collection and she was like — but she stood up and she was great. And it was a great feeling ‘cause the guys dug her and they saw she was the real thing and she respected them and she was prepared. I had fun on that first record.
